## What you will learn

The **haplotype catalogue** turns a `GenoMeta` plus a trait's marker effects
into per-sample, per-block local GEBVs (genomic estimated breeding values) and a
set of diagnostic plots. This example covers:

1. Starting from a **saved `GenoMeta` `.rds` file** (the usual hand-off point).
2. Computing **local GEBVs** with `compute_profile_localgebv()`.
3. **Effect** and **variance** Manhattan plots across the genome.
4. **Haplotype-alignment** plots on chosen subsets (a chromosome, a block set,
   selected samples).
5. Pinning **one row order across every figure** with `use_sample_order()`
   (0.5.5).
6. The one-call orchestrator `run_haplotype_catalogue()`.

```{r load}
library(haploStack)
library(data.table)
```

## 0  Prepare and save a demonstration GenoMeta

The catalogue normally consumes a `GenoMeta` produced earlier (see
*Example 1 — Building a GenoMeta from varying sources*). Here we synthesise a
small population, **save it to an `.rds` file**, and then reload it — mirroring
how you would resume an analysis from a stored object.

```{r make-rds}
set.seed(42)

n_samples <- 16L; n_per_chrom <- 8L; n_chrom <- 3L; block_size <- 4L
n_mk      <- n_per_chrom * n_chrom
markers   <- paste0("M", seq_len(n_mk))
chrom     <- rep(seq_len(n_chrom), each = n_per_chrom)
alleles   <- c("A", "T")                       # nucleotide encoding

# 3-D genotype array: samples × markers × ploidy(2)
arr <- array(sample(alleles, n_samples * n_mk * 2L, replace = TRUE),
             dim = c(n_samples, n_mk, 2L),
             dimnames = list(paste0("S", seq_len(n_samples)), markers, c("1", "2")))

map <- data.frame(
  Chrom  = as.character(chrom),
  Marker = markers,
  Pos    = unlist(lapply(seq_len(n_chrom),
            function(c) sort(sample(seq(1e6, 1e8, 1e5), n_per_chrom)))),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Consecutive markers within a chromosome form a block.
bmm <- data.frame(
  Chrom  = as.character(chrom),
  Marker = markers,
  Block  = unlist(lapply(seq_len(n_chrom),
            function(c) paste0("Chr", c, "_B", ceiling(seq_len(n_per_chrom) / block_size)))),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# One additive effect per (marker, allele).
effects <- data.frame(
  Marker = rep(markers, each = 2L),
  Allele = rep(alleles, times = n_mk),
  Effect = round(rnorm(n_mk * 2L, 0, 0.5), 3),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

meta <- new_geno_meta(
  geno_arrays           = arr,
  map_info              = map,
  block_marker_map_info = bmm,
  metadata = list(ploidy = 2L, char_dict = c("A" = 1L, "T" = 2L),
                  n_samples = n_samples, n_markers = n_mk,
                  source_format = "simulated", encoding = "nucleotide"),
  marker_effects = effects)

rds_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "catalogue_demo.rds")
save_geno_meta(meta, rds_path)
```

```{r load-rds}
# === The catalogue workflow begins here, from a saved object ===
meta <- load_geno_meta(rds_path)
is_geno_meta(meta)

cat("Samples:", meta$metadata$n_samples,
    "| Markers:", meta$metadata$n_markers,
    "| Blocks:", length(unique(meta$block_marker_map_info$Block)), "\n")
```

---

## 1  Compute local GEBVs

`compute_profile_localgebv()` returns a wide **Block × Sample** `data.table`.
With `level = "genotype"` the two haplotypes of each sample are summed;
`center = "allele_freq"` expresses each value relative to the population mean.
The marker effects stored on the object are used automatically.

```{r gebv}
gebv <- compute_profile_localgebv(meta, level = "genotype", center = "allele_freq")

dim(gebv)                              # n_blocks × (n_samples + 1 Block column)
gebv[, 1:6]
```

A quick per-sample ranking by total GEBV:

```{r gebv-summary}
sample_cols <- setdiff(names(gebv), "Block")
totals <- data.table(Sample = sample_cols,
                     TotalGEBV = colSums(gebv[, ..sample_cols], na.rm = TRUE))
head(totals[order(-TotalGEBV)])
```

---

## 2  Genome-wide visualisation

Both Manhattan helpers need genomic coordinates, so first build a block-location
table (`Block, Chrom, Pos, …`) and reshape the GEBV matrix to long form.

```{r block-loc}
bloc <- as.data.table(build_block_location_info(meta)$block_info)
bloc[, .(Block, Chrom, Start, End, Pos, Num_SNPs)]

long_gebv <- melt(gebv, id.vars = "Block",
                  variable.name = "Sample", value.name = "Effect")
long_gebv <- merge(long_gebv, bloc[, .(Block, Chrom, Pos)], by = "Block")
```

### 2.1  Effect Manhattan — per-sample block effects

Each point is one sample's local GEBV at one block, placed at the block's
genomic position. Useful for spotting blocks where carriers differ strongly.

```{r manhattan-effect}
p_eff <- plot_manhattan_effect(long_gebv, trait_name = "Demo trait")
print(p_eff)
```

### 2.2  Variance Manhattan — where the population varies

Collapsing to per-block variance of the GEBV highlights the blocks that
discriminate most between samples (the natural targets for stacking).

```{r manhattan-variance}
block_var <- long_gebv[, .(BlockVariance = var(Effect, na.rm = TRUE)),
                       by = .(Block, Chrom, Pos)]
p_var <- plot_manhattan_variance(block_var, trait_name = "Demo trait")
print(p_var)
```

---

## 3  Haplotype alignment on specific subsets

`plot_haplotype_alignment()` draws every sample's two haplotypes as coloured
marker tracks. The figure carries two column-level groupings: **chromosomes**
are sub-panels (one facet column each, as wide as its share of the markers) and
**blocks** are annotated inside each panel — dot-dash boundaries plus vertical
block IDs hanging from the panel top.

```{r align-genome, fig.height=6, fig.width=10}
plot_haplotype_alignment(meta, method = "genotype")
```

Whole-genome alignments are dense, so subset with `filter_geno_meta()` — by
chromosome, by block, or by sample — when you want to read individual markers.
`chrom_panels = FALSE` returns the pre-0.5.0 figure: one continuous marker axis
with the chromosomes named only in the subtitle.

### 3.1  One chromosome

A single-chromosome panel is never faceted; the `Chr …` subtitle names it.

```{r align-chrom, fig.height=6}
meta_chr1 <- filter_geno_meta(meta, chromosomes = list(list(chr = "1")))
plot_haplotype_alignment(meta_chr1,
                         show_block_boundaries = TRUE,
                         show_block_labels     = TRUE)
```

### 3.2  A chosen set of blocks, for a subset of samples

```{r align-blocks, fig.height=5}
top_blocks <- block_var[order(-BlockVariance)][1:3, Block]   # 3 most-variable blocks
elite      <- paste0("S", 1:6)

meta_sub <- filter_geno_meta(meta, keep_samples = elite, blocks = top_blocks)
plot_haplotype_alignment(meta_sub,
                         show_block_boundaries = TRUE,
                         show_block_labels     = TRUE,
                         show_individual_names = TRUE)
```

### 3.3  One row order for every figure — `use_sample_order()`

Each figure with a sample axis used to pick its own row order: alphabetical
here, family history there, ggplot2's discrete scale elsewhere. Two panels of
the same population could therefore put the same line on different rows, and
`plot_meta_alignment()` *hid* it — it imposes the first panel's axis on the
rest, so a mismatched pair still rendered, silently re-ordered.

Since 0.5.5 there is one rule:

> A per-call `sample_order` argument wins. Then the broadcast option. Then the
> figure's own default.

`cluster_samples()` produces a dendrogram leaf order; `use_sample_order()`
broadcasts it to every figure in the session and returns the previous value, so
a script can put it back.

```{r sample-order, fig.height=6, fig.width=10}
cl  <- cluster_samples(meta, k = 2)
old <- use_sample_order(cl)          # broadcast; returns the previous setting

plot_haplotype_alignment(meta, method = "genotype")
```

The subtitle now carries the ordering provenance (`rows: ward.D2 / hamming,
k=2`), so a clustered panel cannot be mistaken for an alphabetical one. Each
figure also records what it drew:

```{r sample-order-attrs}
p <- plot_haplotype_alignment(meta, method = "genotype")
attr(p, "sample_order_source")       # "default" | "argument" | "option"
head(attr(p, "sample_order"))
```

Two asymmetries are worth knowing:

- An order passed **as an argument** must be a permutation of that panel's
  samples — a mismatch is an error, because you named those samples for that
  figure.
- A **broadcast** order is best-effort: it is intersected with whatever the
  panel holds, and panel samples missing from it are appended after the ordered
  ones. Without that, one `use_sample_order()` call would turn every filtered
  panel in the session into an error at a distance.

An order never moves a sample between groups. In the family-faceted figures the
offspring/founder split and its dashed boundary stay put; rows are re-arranged
only *inside* each group. Haplotype-level panels keep a sample's copies adjacent
(`S1.1`, `S1.2`), so re-ordering moves whole samples, never single copies.
Blocks are untouched — the column axis stays in genomic order.

Clear the broadcast when you are done, or every later figure in the session
inherits it:

```{r sample-order-clear}
use_sample_order(old)                # `old` is NULL if nothing was set before
```

Composing panels, `plot_meta_alignment(check_order = TRUE)` (the default) warns
when panels disagree rather than re-ordering them silently. The fix is to draw
both from the same order — usually by broadcasting one.

---

## 4  One-call catalogue — `run_haplotype_catalogue()`

For a (multi-trait) production run, `run_haplotype_catalogue()` wraps GEBV
computation, per-sample summaries, block counts, the long block catalogue, and
plot/file export into a single call. Pass effects as a **named list** (one
element per trait).

```{r catalogue}
out_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "catalogue_out")

results <- run_haplotype_catalogue(
  geno_meta    = meta,
  effect_list  = list(Demo = effects),     # add more named traits here
  output_dir   = out_dir,
  save_profile = TRUE,                      # writes the GenoMeta .rds too
  n_cores      = 1L
)

names(results)                              # one element per trait
names(results$Demo)                         # gebv_matrix, gebv_summary, block_counts, ...
```

The per-trait `block_counts` table feeds a ready-made stacked bar chart of how
many blocks carry a positive / zero / negative effect in each sample:

```{r block-counts, fig.height=5}
plot_block_counts(results$Demo$block_counts, trait_name = "Demo")
```

Files written to the output directory (GEBV matrices, summaries, the long
catalogue, and PNG plots):

```{r list-outputs}
list.files(out_dir)
```

---

## 5  Cross-trait block analysis — `analyze_block_catalogue()`

`run_haplotype_catalogue()` is **per-trait**. To compare blocks **across several
traits at once** — which blocks are commonly good, which are trait-specific, and
which carry trade-offs — use `analyze_block_catalogue()`. It works in three
load-bearing steps:

1. **Normalize within each trait.** Each trait's subtype effects are put on a
   common scale (`normalize = "zscore"` is a **true standard score**
   `(x − mean)/sd`, so `0` means an *average*-effect subtype for that trait).
2. **Select one subtype per block, shared across traits.** A **subtype** is a
   specific allele combination; its identity is trait-invariant but its effect
   differs per trait. Each block is represented by the *single* subtype with the
   **highest summed value across traits**,
   `argmax_subtype Σ_t w_t · value(subtype, t)`, where `value` is the raw effect
   `S` or the normalized `N` chosen by **`value_source`**, and `trait_weights`
   are **signed direction only**.
3. **Report each trait's own value.** The selected subtype's per-trait `S` and
   `N` are returned side by side (no composite score), so trade-offs stay visible.

```{r xtrait-data}
# A second trait on a deliberately different scale (so normalisation matters).
set.seed(7)
effects2 <- data.frame(
  Marker = rep(markers, each = 2L),
  Allele = rep(alleles, times = n_mk),
  Effect = round(rnorm(n_mk * 2L, 0, 3), 3),    # ~6x the spread of `effects`
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

ana <- analyze_block_catalogue(
  geno_meta    = meta,
  effect_list  = list(Yield = effects, Protein = effects2),
  fitness_fn   = "max_effect",   # candidate value = the subtype's effect
  normalize    = "zscore",       # within-trait standard score
  value_source = "normalized",   # sum standard scores so the large-scale
                                 # trait does not dominate the selection
  plots        = c("rectangular", "manhattan", "density", "heatmap"))

names(ana)
```

Each block is now represented by **one** subtype, identical across every trait:

```{r xtrait-selected}
head(ana$selected[, .(Block, Subtype, Count, Chrom, Pos)])
```

Its per-trait **raw** effect `S` and **normalized** value `N` are returned as
tidy `Block × Trait` tables (both keyed to that one selected subtype), with a
per-trait top-block flag `is_top`:

```{r xtrait-SN}
head(ana$S[, .(Block, Trait, Subtype, S, is_top)])
head(ana$N[, .(Block, Trait, Subtype, N, is_top)])
```

> **Mixed scales, one honest selection.** Compare `value_source = "raw"` — where
> the wide-spread `Protein` trait dominates the summed selection — with
> `value_source = "normalized"` above, which sums standard scores so neither trait
> swamps the other. Because the analysis reports **each trait's own value** rather
> than a single composite, a block that is good for one trait but poor for another
> stays visible. Use signed `trait_weights` (e.g. `c(Yield = 1, Protein = -1)`) to
> treat a trait as lower-is-better.

The plots are returned in `ana$plots` and **fill by the `value_source` chosen at
analysis time** (D2), so no re-specification is needed; `circos` is a base plot
when the optional *circlize* package is installed, else a linear fallback:

```{r xtrait-genome, fig.height=4}
ana$plots$rectangular     # genome: position x trait, fill = selected subtype's N
ggsave(filename = file.path(out_dir, "cross_trait_rectangular.png"), width = 9, height = 4)
```

```{r xtrait-manhattan, fig.height=6}
ana$plots$manhattan       # one Manhattan panel per trait, top blocks labelled

```

```{r xtrait-density, fig.height=4}
ana$plots$density         # distribution of selected-subtype values per trait
```

Any standalone plotter accepts a `value_source` override, so you can re-plot the
**raw** effect from a `normalized`-selected result without recomputing:

```{r xtrait-genome-raw, fig.height=4}
plot_block_effect_genome(ana, value_source = "raw")   # white = zero effect
```

```{r xtrait-circos, eval=requireNamespace("circlize", quietly = TRUE), fig.height=6}
# One block-effect ring per trait on the circos engine (requires the optional
# 'circlize' package). plot_block_effect_circos() is deprecated since 0.9.0;
# its chord links return as a "links" track of the engine in 0.9.x.
rings <- lapply(unique(as.character(ana$S$Trait)),
                function(tr) track_block_effect(ana, trait = tr))
plot_meta_circos(rings, meta = meta)
```

---

## Summary

| Goal | Function |
|------|----------|
| Resume from a saved object | `load_geno_meta()` |
| Per-block local GEBVs | `compute_profile_localgebv()` |
| Block genomic coordinates | `build_block_location_info()` |
| Effect / variance Manhattan | `plot_manhattan_effect()`, `plot_manhattan_variance()` |
| Subset before plotting | `filter_geno_meta()` |
| Haplotype alignment | `plot_haplotype_alignment()` |
| Whole catalogue + files | `run_haplotype_catalogue()`, `plot_block_counts()` |
| Cross-trait block comparison | `analyze_block_catalogue()` |
| Cross-trait figures | `plot_block_effect_genome()`, `plot_block_effect_manhattan()`, `plot_block_effect_density()`, `plot_top_block_heatmap()`, `plot_block_effect_circos()` |

The local-GEBV matrix produced here is exactly what the stacking simulation
(*Example 4*) selects on.

```{r session}
sessionInfo()
```
